changes.after: Require a type to support equality before comparing its values.

before: A generic parameter names a type chosen at each call. A constraint says which operations that type must support. Equatable promises equality comparison; it does not make every pair equal.

sameEnds accepts an array whose elements share one type T and returns Bool. The where clause T: Equatable permits == inside the body; <T: Equatable> is another spelling of this single constraint. first and last are optional endpoints; guard unwraps both or returns false for an empty array. This reads the array without changing it. A one-element array has equal endpoints. print sends the returned value to standard output.

```swift
func sameEnds<T>(_ values: [T]) -> Bool where T: Equatable {
    guard let first = values.first, let last = values.last else {
        return false
    }
    return first == last
}
print(sameEnds([4, 9, 4]))
print(sameEnds(["oak", "elm"]))
```
Expected output:
```text
true
false
```

after: A generic function can work with several types. A constraint is a rule about the types it accepts. Equatable means the type supports checking whether two values are equal with ==.

where T: Equatable requires that ability from T. The array's items all use T, so the function can compare its first and last items. This requirement allows comparison; it does not make every pair equal.

first and last are optional because an array may be empty. guard let reads both when they exist. For an empty array, return false. A one-item array has the same first and last item, so this comparison returns true.
Swift rejects a call if its item type does not support Equatable. A custom type must provide that ability before this function can use == on its values.
Complete sameEnds without changing the input array. Compare only the first and last items. The middle items do not need to match. Keep false for an empty array.
